claim: African trypanosomes possess hundreds of variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) genes.
source: African trypanosomes possess hundreds of variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) genes, but only one is expressed from a telomeric expression site (ES) at any given time.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citation to Berriman et al., 2005 in the introduction.

claim: Only one VSG gene is expressed from a telomeric expression site (ES) at any given time in African trypanosomes.
source: African trypanosomes possess hundreds of variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) genes, but only one is expressed from a telomeric expression site (ES) at any given time.
evidence: This is a fundamental characteristic of VSG expression stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Expression of a second VSG alone is sufficient to silence the active VSG gene.
source: We found that the expression of a second VSG alone is sufficient to silence the active VSG gene and directionally attenuate the ES by disruptor of telomeric silencing-1B (DOT1B)-mediated histone methylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Expression of a second VSG directionally attenuates the ES by DOT1B-mediated histone methylation.
source: We found that the expression of a second VSG alone is sufficient to silence the active VSG gene and directionally attenuate the ES by disruptor of telomeric silencing-1B (DOT1B)-mediated histone methylation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments comparing wild-type and DOT1B-knockout cells shown in Figure 4.

claim: Three conserved expression-site-associated genes (ESAGs) serve as signal for ES attenuation.
source: Three conserved expression-site-associated genes (ESAGs) appear to serve as signal for ES attenuation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNAi experiments in Figure 7 showing that depletion of ESAGs 1, 2, and 8 causes specific phenotypes.

claim: Depletion of ESAGs 1, 2, and 8 causes G1-phase dormancy.
source: Their depletion causes G1-phase dormancy and reversible initiation of the slender-to-stumpy differentiation pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated through RNAi experiments shown in Figure 7 and growth analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Depletion of ESAGs 1, 2, and 8 causes reversible initiation of the slender-to-stumpy differentiation pathway.
source: Their depletion causes G1-phase dormancy and reversible initiation of the slender-to-stumpy differentiation pathway.
evidence: This is supported by PAD1 expression data in Figures 5 and 7, and the reversibility is shown in growth curves.

claim: ES-attenuated slender bloodstream trypanosomes gain full developmental competence for transformation to the tsetse fly stage.
source: ES-attenuated slender bloodstream trypanosomes gain full developmental competence for transformation to the tsetse fly stage.
evidence: This is demonstrated through cis-aconitate treatment experiments showing EP1 expression and morphological changes in Figure 6.

claim: Each olfactory sensory neuron expresses only one olfactory receptor (OR) from a family of ~1200 genes.
source: In the mammalian central nervous system, each olfactory sensory neuron expresses only one olfactory receptor (OR) from a family of ∼1200 genes (Buck and Axel, 1991).
evidence: This is cited from Buck and Axel, 1991.

claim: Before an OR gene is expressed, all alleles are silenced and converted to heterochromatin.
source: Before an OR gene is expressed, all alleles are silenced and converted to heterochromatin (Magklara et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Magklara et al., 2011.

claim: A limiting enzymatic activity stochastically removes heterochromatin marks from one OR allele to activate it.
source: A limiting enzymatic activity then stochastically removes the heterochromatin marks from one allele to activate it.
evidence: This is part of the description of the OR system mechanism in the introduction.

claim: The expressed OR protein mediates a feedback loop that inhibits removal of heterochromatin marks from all other alleles.
source: The expressed OR protein mediates a feedback loop that inhibits removal of heterochromatin marks from all other alleles, preventing their transcription (Serizawa et al., 2003; Lyons et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Serizawa et al., 2003 and Lyons et al., 2013.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum expresses only one out of 60 members of the var gene family.
source: The malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, for example, expresses only one out of 60 members of the var gene family, each coding for different versions of the surface virulence factor PfEMP1 (Guizetti and Scherf, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Guizetti and Scherf, 2013.

claim: The trypanosome cell surface is covered with millions of copies of VSG that form a dense layer virtually impervious to host-derived antibodies.
source: In the mammalian host, the cell surface is covered with millions of copies of VSG that form a dense layer that is virtually impervious to host-derived antibodies (Cross, 1975; Engstler et al., 2007; Schwede et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Cross, 1975; Engstler et al., 2007; and Schwede et al., 2011.

claim: VSGs are highly immunogenic and provoke a rapid and efficient immune response that diminishes the parasite population.
source: VSGs are highly immunogenic and provoke a rapid and efficient immune response that diminishes the parasite population.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Trypanosomes that have successfully switched to expression of another VSG survive immune clearance.
source: Only trypanosomes that have successfully switched to expression of another, structurally similar but immunologically distinct VSG survive.
evidence: This is stated as part of the antigenic variation mechanism in the introduction.

claim: Trypanosomes possess several hundred VSG genes.
source: Trypanosomes possess several hundred VSG genes (Berriman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Berriman et al., 2005.

claim: VSG genes are expressed from one of ~15 telomeric expression sites (ES).
source: VSG genes are expressed from one of ∼15 telomeric expression sites (ES) but only one of these is transcribed at any given time (Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008.

claim: Chromatin remodeling plays an important role in maintaining monoallelic expression of the active ES.
source: Chromatin remodeling appears to play an important role in maintaining the monoallelic expression of the active ES (Horn and McCulloch, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Horn and McCulloch, 2010.

claim: Antigenic variation can result from a change in the active ES through gene conversion at the VSG locus.
source: Antigenic variation can result from either a change in the active ES, usually gene conversion at the VSG locus, or by an epigenetic change that results in silencing of the active ES and transcription of a previously silent ES (in situ switch).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about antigenic variation mechanisms.

claim: Antigenic variation can result from an epigenetic change that silences the active ES and transcribes a previously silent ES (in situ switch).
source: Antigenic variation can result from either a change in the active ES, usually gene conversion at the VSG locus, or by an epigenetic change that results in silencing of the active ES and transcription of a previously silent ES (in situ switch).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about antigenic variation mechanisms.

claim: No mechanism or factor has been identified that is involved in the initiation of in situ switching prior to this study.
source: No mechanism or factor has been identified that is involved in the initiation of the latter.
evidence: This statement establishes the novelty of the current findings.

claim: The trypanosome bloodstream form ES is exclusively functional in the proliferating slender bloodstream stage.
source: Consequently, the trypanosome bloodstream form ES is exclusively functional in the proliferating slender bloodstream stage of the parasite.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ES function during the life cycle.

claim: Trypanosomes differentiate to the quiescent stumpy form in response to quorum sensing.
source: In response to quorum sensing, the trypanosomes differentiate to the quiescent stumpy form.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about trypanosome development.

claim: Stumpy forms are competent for developmental transition to procyclic forms after ingestion by a tsetse fly.
source: Stumpy forms are competent for the next developmental transition to procyclic forms, which occurs after ingestion by a tsetse fly (Reuner et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from Reuner et al., 1997.

claim: Developmental transition from stumpy to procyclic is accompanied by silencing of the active ES.
source: This developmental transition is accompanied by silencing of the active ES so that allelic exclusion is lost.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ES behavior during development.

claim: VSG121 mRNA reached 82(±1)% of wild type levels within 2 hr of tetracycline induction.
source: Quantitative Northern blot analysis revealed an almost instantaneous increase of VSG121 mRNA, reaching 82(±1)% of wild type levels within 2 hr (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly measured and quantified from Northern blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Endogenous VSG221 transcripts declined with kinetics compatible with mRNA half-life after VSG121 induction.
source: This was followed by a reduction of endogenous VSG221 transcripts, which declined with kinetics compatible with the mRNA half-life (Ehlers et al., 1987).
evidence: This is observed in the data in Figure 1B and compared to published mRNA half-life data from Ehlers et al., 1987.

claim: Total VSG mRNA initially peaked at 180% but leveled to approximately wild-type quantities within 8 hr.
source: The total VSG mRNA initially peaked at 180%, but within 8 hr leveled to approximately wild-type quantities.
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The VSG mRNA population was effectively exchanged within 8 hr of VSG121 induction.
source: Thus, the VSG mRNA population was effectively exchanged in this time period.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetics data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: VSG121 protein was detectable within 4–6 hr after induction.
source: The VSG121 protein was detectable within 4–6 hr after induction (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is measured from protein quantification data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: After 24 hr of VSG121 induction, the surface coat of all cells was dominated by VSG121.
source: After 24 hr, the surface coat of all cells was dominated by VSG121 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and the amount of VSG221 had declined to 21(±2)% (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: The amount of VSG221 declined to 21(±2)% after 24 hr of VSG121 induction.
source: After 24 hr, the surface coat of all cells was dominated by VSG121 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and the amount of VSG221 had declined to 21(±2)% (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is quantified from protein data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: mRNAs from telomere proximal ESAG1 and 2 genes decreased faster than mRNA from telomere distal ESAG12 gene.
source: It appears that mRNAs from the telomere proximal ESAG1 and 2 genes decreased faster than mRNA from the telomere distal ESAG12 gene.
evidence: This is observed from the ESAG mRNA quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Promoter proximal GFP mRNA decreased with significantly slower kinetics than promoter distal GFP mRNA upon VSG121 induction.
source: Upon induction of VSG121 expression, the promoter proximal GFP mRNA decreased with significantly slower kinetics (p<0.018; two-way ANOVA test) than that of the promoter distal GFP (Figure 2C, left panel), revealing that the kinetics of GFP mRNA reduction was determined solely by the position of the GFP gene within the active ES.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally with GFP reporters at different ES positions and quantified in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: The kinetics of GFP mRNA reduction was determined solely by the position of the GFP gene within the active ES.
source: Upon induction of VSG121 expression, the promoter proximal GFP mRNA decreased with significantly slower kinetics (p<0.018; two-way ANOVA test) than that of the promoter distal GFP (Figure 2C, left panel), revealing that the kinetics of GFP mRNA reduction was determined solely by the position of the GFP gene within the active ES.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential kinetics of GFP reporters at different positions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VSG121 overexpression caused a gradual loss of ES activity that started at the telomere and propagated towards the VSG promoter.
source: Thus, VSG121 overexpression caused a gradual loss of ES activity that started at the telomere and propagated towards the VSG promoter.
evidence: This is concluded from the position-dependent kinetics of gene silencing shown in Figure 2.

claim: ES attenuation was completed within one cell division cycle.
source: This process was completed within one cell division cycle and was maintained for 120 hr (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is observed from the kinetics data in Figure 1B.

claim: The ES was gradually reactivated in the reverse direction after 120 hr.
source: Then the ES was gradually reactivated in the reverse direction (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by the GFP reporter kinetics in Figure 2C.

claim: The ES was not silenced completely, representing ES attenuation rather than bona fide ES silencing.
source: The ES was not silenced completely, so the effect did not constitute a bona fide ES silencing, but a fine-tuned ES attenuation.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that ES activity decreased to ~20% but not to zero.

claim: Parasite growth was not affected for the first 24 hr of VSG121 induction.
source: Parasite growth was not affected for the first 24 hr of tetracycline induction, but then cell proliferation slowed down significantly (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the growth curve data in Figure 3A.

claim: Cell proliferation slowed down significantly after 24 hr of VSG121 induction.
source: Parasite growth was not affected for the first 24 hr of tetracycline induction, but then cell proliferation slowed down significantly (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the growth curve data in Figure 3A.

claim: Cell cycle analysis showed an accumulation of 1K1N cells with pre-replication kinetoplast morphology after VSG121 induction.
source: The cell cycle was analyzed by determining the nucleus (N) and kinetoplast (K) configuration and showed an accumulation of 1K1N cells with the kinetoplasts having a pre-replication morphology and a reduction of cells containing a dividing kinetoplast (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is shown by cell cycle analysis data in Figure 3B,C.

claim: There was a reduction of cells containing a dividing kinetoplast after VSG121 induction.
source: The cell cycle was analyzed by determining the nucleus (N) and kinetoplast (K) configuration and showed an accumulation of 1K1N cells with the kinetoplasts having a pre-replication morphology and a reduction of cells containing a dividing kinetoplast (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is shown by cell cycle analysis data in Figure 3B,C.

claim: After 24 hr of VSG121 expression, only 17% of trypanosomes entered nuclear S-phase within a 4-hr labeling window.
source: In contrast, after 24 hr of VSG121 expression only 17% incorporated EdU into nuclear DNA within an equivalent 4-hr window.
evidence: This is measured from EdU incorporation experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When parasites were incubated with EdU for 18 hr after 24 hr of VSG121 expression, 86% had entered S-phase.
source: However, when the parasites were incubated with EdU for 18 hr, 86% had entered S-phase.
evidence: This is measured from EdU incorporation experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The cells showed a specific, at least fivefold expansion of the G1-phase from 3 to 15 hr.
source: Thus, the cells were clearly not arrested in the cell cycle, but showed a specific, at least fivefold expansion of the G1-phase from 3 to 15 hr.
evidence: This is calculated from the EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: All trypanosomes remained fully motile and no morphological abnormality or cell death was observed during ES attenuation.
source: Remarkably, all trypanosomes remained fully motile and no morphological abnormality or cell death was observed.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After 8 hr of tetracycline induction, the general transcription rate was not impaired.
source: After 8 hr of tetracycline induction, when VSG221 transcripts had already decreased to 20%, the general transcription rate was not impaired at all.
evidence: This is measured by BrUTP incorporation shown in Figure 3E.

claim: After 24 hr of tetracycline induction, global transcription was reduced to 30%.
source: Only after 24 hr was the global transcription reduced to 30% (p<0.0001; unpaired t test) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is measured by BrUTP incorporation shown in Figure 3E with statistical significance.

claim: ES attenuation precedes growth retardation and general transcriptional diminution.
source: This formally proves that ES attenuation precedes growth retardation and general transcriptional diminution.
evidence: This is concluded from the temporal sequence of events shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Both RNA polymerase I and II transcription were affected by ES attenuation.
source: To test if RNA polymerase I and II transcription was both affected, we inserted luciferase reporter transgenes either downstream of an rDNA promoter or into the tubulin-locus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). In both the cases, luciferase activity was down to 30–50% within 2 days.
evidence: This is demonstrated with luciferase reporters driven by different polymerases shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Luciferase activity from both Pol I and Pol II promoters was down to 30–50% within 2 days of VSG121 induction.
source: To test if RNA polymerase I and II transcription was both affected, we inserted luciferase reporter transgenes either downstream of an rDNA promoter or into the tubulin-locus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). In both the cases, luciferase activity was down to 30–50% within 2 days.
evidence: This is measured from luciferase assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DOT1B is involved in the silencing of the active ES during in situ switching.
source: The histone methyltransferase DOT1B is involved in the silencing of the active ES during in situ switching (Figueiredo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Figueiredo et al., 2008.

claim: In DOT1B-deleted cells, VSG221 protein decreased with the same kinetics as in parental cells following VSG121 induction.
source: Following induction of VSG121 expression, the decrease of the ES-resident VSG221 protein occurred with the same kinetics as in the parental cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by protein quantification in DOT1B knockout cells in Figure 4A.

claim: DOT1B-deleted cells did not display a growth phenotype after VSG121 induction.
source: Furthermore, the cells did not display a growth phenotype (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the growth curve for DOT1B knockout cells in Figure 4B.

claim: In DOT1B-knockout trypanosomes, luciferase activity was only marginally and transiently reduced at day 2.
source: However, in the DOT1B-knockout trypanosomes luciferase activity was only marginally and transiently reduced at day 2 (Figure 4C, left panel).
evidence: This is measured from luciferase assays in DOT1B knockout cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In DOT1B-deleted cells, the ES was not attenuated except for the most telomere-proximal part where the VSG221 gene resides.
source: Thus, in DOT1B-deleted cells, the ES was not attenuated, except for the most telomere-proximal part, where the VSG221 gene resides.
evidence: This is concluded from the luciferase reporter data in DOT1B knockout cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Silencing of a VSG gene can be uncoupled from ES silencing.
source: This suggests that silencing of a VSG gene can be uncoupled from ES silencing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that VSG221 is silenced but the ES is not attenuated in DOT1B knockout cells.

claim: ES attenuation requires DOT1B-dependent histone tri-methylation.
source: While ES attenuation seems to require DOT1B-dependent histone tri-methylation, VSG silencing does not.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects in DOT1B knockout cells shown in Figure 4.

claim: VSG silencing does not require DOT1B-dependent histone tri-methylation.
source: While ES attenuation seems to require DOT1B-dependent histone tri-methylation, VSG silencing does not.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that VSG221 is silenced in DOT1B knockout cells shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ES-resident VSG can be complemented in trans by a heterologous VSG gene.
source: Furthermore, these results formally prove that the ES-resident VSG can be complemented in trans by a heterologous VSG gene.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that cells survive with VSG121 expression while VSG221 is silenced.

claim: High-level expression of a second VSG is sufficient to attenuate and eventually silence the formerly active ES.
source: We conclude that the activation of a new VSG ES initiates an in situ switch, and that high-level expression of a second VSG is sufficient to attenuate and eventually silence the formerly active ES.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the experiments shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: PAD1 protein was detectable on the surface of trypanosomes in G1-phase after 48 hr of VSG121 overexpression.
source: After 48 hr of VSG121 overexpression, however, the PAD1 protein was clearly detectable on the surface of trypanosomes in the G1-phase of the cell cycle (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The GFP:PADutr reporter was visible in most G1 cells after 48 hr of VSG121 overexpression.
source: Likewise, the GFP:PADutr reporter was visible in most G1 cells, but was also expressed in a minor portion of trypanosomes in other cell cycle phases (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry and microscopy in Figure 5C.

claim: VSG overexpression-induced ES attenuation triggers G1-phase prolongation and expression of PAD1 in monomorphic slender stage trypanosomes.
source: We conclude that in the absence of the quorum-sensing factor SIF and at 37°C, the VSG overexpression-induced ES attenuation triggers G1-phase prolongation and concomitant expression of a bona fide stumpy marker in monomorphic slender stage trypanosomes.
evidence: This is concluded from the PAD1 expression and cell cycle data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: PAD1 expression was induced despite global transcriptional attenuation.
source: Notably, PAD1 expression was induced despite the global transcriptional attenuation that started at the same time.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the timing of PAD1 induction (Figure 5) with global transcription reduction (Figure 3E).

claim: ES-attenuated trypanosomes became sensitive to cis-aconitate and expressed EP1 on the cell surface.
source: We induced VSG121 expression for 48 hr and then incubated the trypanosomes in the absence of tetracycline with 6 mM cis-aconitate. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed EP1 surface expression as early as 6 hr after addition of cis-aconitate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 24 hr of cis-aconitate treatment, 70(±6)% of ES-attenuated cells were EP1-positive.
source: After 24 hr, 70(±6)% of cells were EP1-positive (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is quantified from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: ES-attenuated trypanosomes altered their cell architecture, adopting a stumpy-like morphology after cis-aconitate treatment.
source: Furthermore, the trypanosomes also altered their cell architecture, adopting a stumpy-like morphology after 6 hr of cis-aconitate treatment.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 24 hr of cis-aconitate treatment, the posterior part of ES-attenuated cells had elongated and the kinetoplast had repositioned and segregated.
source: After 24 hr, the posterior part of the cells had elongated and the kinetoplast had repositioned and segregated (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 27°C, after 6 hr of cis-aconitate treatment, 58(±8)% of ES-attenuated cells revealed strong EP1 fluorescence on the cell surface.
source: After 6 hr, 58(±8)% of cells revealed strong EP1 fluorescence on the cell surface, while only 5(±2)% of the control population were EP1-positive (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is quantified from flow cytometry data at 27°C shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: ES-attenuated trypanosomes accelerated the cell cycle after 24 hr at 27°C and started growing as procyclic trypanosomes.
source: Interestingly, the ES-attenuated trypanosomes accelerated the cell cycle after 24 hr and started growing as procyclic trypanosomes (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in the growth curve at 27°C in Figure 6F.

claim: ESAG1-RNAi reduced transcript levels to 30%.
source: It should be mentioned that ESAG1-RNAi reduced transcript levels to only 30%, while ESAG2-RNAi was more effective and reduced the mRNA to less than 5%, which may explain the lethal phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in the Northern blot data in Figure 7A.

claim: ESAG2-RNAi reduced mRNA to less than 5%.
source: It should be mentioned that ESAG1-RNAi reduced transcript levels to only 30%, while ESAG2-RNAi was more effective and reduced the mRNA to less than 5%, which may explain the lethal phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in the Northern blot data in Figure 7C.

claim: ESAG1-RNAi caused transient growth impairment at days 2 and 3.
source: Growth was significantly but transiently impaired at days 2 and 3 of RNAi (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in the growth curve in Figure 7A.

claim: ESAG1-RNAi caused accumulation of GFP-positive cells after 48 hr with a peak at day 3.
source: Whereas no GFP was detected in the first 24 hr, there was an accumulation of GFP-positive cells after 48 hr and a peak of GFP expression at day 3.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 7B.

claim: ESAG2-RNAi caused cell growth to stop after 3 days and parasites started to die.
source: After 3 days, GFP was detected in 75% of all cells. At this time, cell growth stopped and the parasites started to die (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is shown in the growth curve and flow cytometry in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Only ablation of ESAGs 1, 2, and 8 induced PAD1 expression.
source: In addition to ESAG1 and 2, only ablation of ESAG8 caused PAD1 induction, albeit in a less pronounced manner.
evidence: This is shown by comparing RNAi effects on different ESAGs in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Down-regulation of ESAGs 3, 6, 7, and 12 was not accompanied by PAD1 expression.
source: The distinctive growth phenotypes observed after down-regulation of ESAGs 3, 6, 7, and 12 were not accompanied by PAD1 expression at any time (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Starting at day 5 of VSG121 induction, the attenuation of the VSG221 ES was gradually lifted.
source: Starting at day 5 of VSG121 induction, the attenuation of the VSG221 ES was gradually lifted.
evidence: This is shown in the kinetics data in Figures 1B and 2C.

claim: The kinetics of ES re-activation was directional, starting at the promoter and proceeding towards the telomere.
source: Interestingly, the kinetics of ES re-activation was also directional, starting at the promoter and proceeding towards the telomere.
evidence: This is shown by the GFP reporter kinetics in Figure 2C.

claim: VSG221 mRNA slowly increased to pre-induction levels between days 5 and 8.
source: VSG221 mRNA slowly increased to pre-induction levels between days 5 and 8 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the mRNA quantification in Figure 1B.

claim: At day 8, the VSG221 surface coat had returned and VSG121 was back to pre-induction levels.
source: At day 8, the VSG221 surface coat had returned and VSG121 was back to pre-induction levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the protein quantification in Figure 1B.

claim: At day 10, population doubling times were back to normal (6 hr).
source: With onset of VSG ES reactivation, the G1-retardation was lifted, cell cycle progression was accelerated, and at day 10, the population doubling times were back to normal (6 hr) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the growth curve in Figure 3A.

claim: All 20 analyzed clonal populations re-activated the VSG221 ES with no indication of ES switching.
source: We have analyzed 20 clonal populations and all clones re-activated the VSG221 ES; no indication of ES switching was found.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from clonal analysis experiments.

claim: More than 20% of the population was responsive to re-induction of VSG121 after 10 days without tetracycline.
source: We cultivated the trypanosomes for an additional 10 days in the absence of tetracycline and then re-induced expression of VSG121. More than 20% of the population was responsive to re-induction and showed strong VSG121 expression, pointing against destructive mutations in the inducible expression system.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from re-induction experiments.

claim: The expressed OR protein mediates a feedback loop that prevents transcription of other OR alleles in the mammalian olfactory system.
source: In the mammalian olfactory receptor (OR) system, the expression of an ectopic OR transgene is sufficient to mediate a feedback inhibition that prevents the expression of the active endogenous OR gene, independent of the receptor signal transduction pathway (Nguyen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Nguyen et al., 2007 and used as a comparison to the VSG system.

claim: The mechanistic principle of feedback inhibition in monoallelic expression appears conserved between kinetoplastids and mammals.
source: This is strongly reminiscent of the VSG-mediated attenuation of the trypanosome ES reported here. Despite the enormous evolutionary distance between kinetoplastids and mammals the mechanistic principle appears to be conserved.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the VSG system to the OR system.

claim: Loss of VSG mRNA by RNAi results in rapid cell cycle arrest.
source: Though the system is optimized for a monotypic coat, two VSGs have to be handled on the same cell surface during antigen switching. Although nothing is known about the length of this period, the different underlying molecular mechanisms suggest variable time scales. Telomere exchange or gene conversion are probably rather fast processes as loss of VSG mRNA by RNAi results in rapid cell cycle arrest (Sheader et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Sheader et al., 2005.

claim: In stable VSG double-expressors with a second VSG inserted upstream of the endogenous copy, both VSGs are expressed in a 50/50 ratio.
source: This model further explains the expression levels in stable VSG double-expressors that have a second VSG inserted into the active ES, just upstream of the endogenous copy (Muñoz-Jordán et al., 1996). In these double-expressors, both VSGs are expressed in a 50/50 ratio, not exceeding a total amount of 100% compared to wild-type single expressors (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments with double-expressor cell lines, citing Muñoz-Jordán et al., 1996.

claim: Generation of VSG double-expressors requires antibiotic selection for 7 days after transfection.
source: The generation of such double-expressors requires antibiotic selection for 7 days after transfection.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological observation.

claim: The trypanosome ES can be regarded as a fine-tuned regulator at the crossroads of antigenic variation, proliferation, and development.
source: Thus, the trypanosome ES can be regarded as a fine-tuned regulator at the crossroads of antigenic variation, proliferation, and development.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the introduction based on the findings presented.

claim: ES attenuation provides a time window for ES quality control.
source: Thus, the concept of transient ES attenuation rather than immediate and complete ES silencing may be of some physiological relevance; it could allow probing for ES performance, for example ESAG functionality, VSG switching orders, quality of novel mosaic VSGs, or newly assembled expression sites.
evidence: This is proposed as a model in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: ES switching plasticity could determine host range in trypanosomes.
source: Provided a sufficiently high ES activation frequency exists, the parasites could effectively probe for host serum-compatible ESAGs (Bitter et al., 1998; Chaves et al., 1999; Pays et al., 2001). Hence, ES switching plasticity could determine the host range.
evidence: This is proposed as a hypothesis in the discussion, citing relevant literature.

claim: Trypanosoma b. rhodesiense is specifically adapted to human serum by expression of the serum-resistance antigen (SRA) from one particular VSG ES.
source: One extreme example for this is Trypanosoma b. rhodesiense, which is human-infective and thought to be a host-range variant of T. b. brucei. The parasites are specifically adapted to human serum by expression of the serum-resistance antigen (SRA) from one particular VSG ES in most isolates.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about T. b. rhodesiense.

claim: The T. b. rhodesiense SRA-containing ES is missing several ESAGs present in all other ESs.
source: The structure of the SRA-containing ES is unusual as it is missing several ESAGs present in all other ESs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the SRA ES structure.

claim: T. b. rhodesiense must not switch off the SRA-containing ES, making the ESAG-dependent differentiation pathway obsolete.
source: During an infection of a human, an in situ switch to a VSG in another ES would cause loss of SRA expression, with lethal consequences. Thus, T. b. rhodesiense must not switch off the SRA-containing ES, thus making the ESAG-dependent differentiation pathway obsolete.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for SRA expression for human infectivity.

claim: The T. b. rhodesiense ES has lost ESAGs 1, 2 and 8.
source: This may be the reason why the T. b. rhodesiense ES has lost ESAG1, 2 and 8.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation based on the findings about ESAG function.

claim: Monomorphic cells used in this study are unresponsive to SIF.
source: The monomorphic cells used in this study are unresponsive to SIF and hence, should have lost the capacity to differentiate to the tsetse-infective stage (Vassella et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the cell line used, citing Vassella et al., 1997.

claim: VSG-induced ES attenuation renders monomorphic trypanosomes fully competent for development in the absence of SIF.
source: In our experiments, however, VSG-induced ES attenuation renders monomorphic trypanosomes fully competent for development.
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated through the cis-aconitate response experiments in Figure 6.

claim: ES attenuation is a reversible process, distinguishing it from SIF-mediated stumpy formation.
source: There is, however, one principal feature that distinguishes SIF-mediated stumpy formation from ES-regulated cell dormancy. While stumpy parasites are terminally differentiated and can only survive if taken up by an insect, the onset of differentiation is fully reversible in the ES-attenuated trypanosomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ES reactivation data shown in Figures 1B and 2C.

claim: ES-attenuated parasites linger in an intermediate state with open developmental choices.
source: We postulate that these parasites linger in an intermediate state with open developmental choices (Figure 8).
evidence: This is proposed as a model based on the reversibility and developmental competence data, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: ES-attenuated parasites can complete ES switching by adapting to the new ES.
source: They have the capacity to complete ES switching by adapting to the new ES or, alternatively, they can re-activate the old, attenuated ES.
evidence: This is proposed as one of the developmental options in the model shown in Figure 8.

claim: ES-attenuated parasites can re-activate the old, attenuated ES.
source: They have the capacity to complete ES switching by adapting to the new ES or, alternatively, they can re-activate the old, attenuated ES.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ES reactivation data in Figures 1B and 2C.

claim: If taken up by the tsetse fly, ES-attenuated parasites would immediately transform to the procyclic insect stage.
source: If taken up by the tsetse fly, however, they would immediately transform to the procyclic insect stage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cis-aconitate response experiments in Figure 6.

claim: The state of the expression site is a fine-tuned module at the crossroads of antigenic variation and development.
source: Thus, the state of the expression site must not be regarded as a simple on-off switch, but rather represents a fine-tuned module at the unexpected crossroads of antigenic variation and development.
evidence: This is the concluding statement summarizing the main findings of the study.
